meta.title: FFCom · your community, on your server
meta.description: FFCom organizes conversation into servers, categories, and text, voice, and forum channels, but each server runs on the machine of whoever creates the community.
meta.ogDescription: Servers and text, voice, and forum channels, hosted by whoever creates the community.

hero.title: Your community, on your server.
hero.lead: FFCom organizes conversation the way you already know: servers, categories, and text, voice, and forum channels. The difference is who keeps all of it, because each server runs on the machine of whoever creates the community, and no company can shut it down, sell it, or change its rules for you.
hero.windowsNote: In the Windows app, the app itself tells you when there is a new version. When installing, Windows may show "Windows protected your PC": click More info and then Run anyway.
hero.androidNote: On Android, the app comes as an APK, outside the Play Store. When you open the file, Android asks you to allow installing apps from this source (the browser or the files app), and Play Protect may warn that the app is unknown: tap More details and then Install anyway. After that, the app itself tells you when there is a new version. Every APK version, with its release notes, is in the app releases on GitHub.

features.title: What already works
features.subtitle: Everything below is already built and live on the test instance.

text.title: Real-time text
text.body: Text channels with history, attachments, message editing and deletion, and unread indicators across all servers at once.

voice.title: Voice, video, and screen
voice.body: Voice channels with camera, screen sharing, push-to-talk, and a mute shortcut, running on a LiveKit that lives on your own server.

forum.title: Forum
forum.body: For what shouldn't get lost in the chat: threads with replies, organized like any other channel.

roles.title: Roles and permissions
roles.body: Roles with per-server permissions and per-channel overrides, plus invites, kicking, and banning members.

friends.title: Friends and direct messages
friends.body: A friends list with presence, and end-to-end encrypted direct messages: not even the server that delivers the message can read it.

apps.title: In the browser or installed
apps.body: Works in the browser and can be installed as an app (PWA). The Electron desktop version is in the works.

how.title: How it works
how.subtitle: There are three pieces, and only one of them is central: the one that keeps your account.
how.centralBody: Login, profile, friends, encrypted direct messages, and the list of servers you've joined. It doesn't store the servers' conversations.
how.clientBody: A single app talks to as many servers as you want, each at the address of whoever hosts it.
how.note: Each server-channel keeps its own channels, messages, files, and voice calls. If one goes down, the others keep working, and no outsider decides who gets in: you only reach a server through an invite or its address.

host.title: Host your own
host.p1: An FFCom server is a directory with a docker-compose.yml and an .env file. It starts the service, the Postgres database, LiveKit for voice and video, and a TURN server to get through NAT, without compiling anything on your machine.
host.p2: Once installed, the server updates itself: it checks a signed release index, verifies the signature and hash of each binary, and rolls back to the previous version if the new one fails to start.
host.p3: Today the image is published for linux/amd64. A reverse proxy with HTTPS goes in front of the server; the guide recommends Caddy, which issues the certificate on its own.

name.title: Why FFCom
name.p1: The people you call without warning deserve a place to talk that is yours, not a space rented from a company that may change the rules tomorrow. That's where FFCom came from: to talk with the people who matter, on a server you control.
name.p2: The logo tells the same story. It is two f letters sharing the same bar, like the classic typographic ligature, inside a speech bubble: the bar running through both is the bond between people.
name.logoAlt: FFCom logo: two lowercase f letters joined by the same bar, inside a speech bubble

status.title: Where we are
status.body: FFCom is being tested with real users on the official instance, and every new account goes through approval: request yours here. The code is public on GitHub under the AGPL-3.0 license, and what is left to do is in the project TODO. Technical decisions, with the alternatives considered and the reason for each choice, are in docs/architecture.md.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.subtitle: What the official FFCom instance stores and where each thing goes.
privacy.account: Account. Your sign-up request (name, username, nickname, email, reason and the IP address it came from) is kept on the central server for review. Once approved, sign-in and password live in the instance's Authentik. The central server stores your profile (display name, avatar and language), your server list, your friends and your direct messages, which are end-to-end encrypted: it only keeps the ciphertext and cannot read them.
privacy.communities: Communities. Each community's messages, attachments and members live on its community server (server-channel), under the control of whoever hosts it, not on the central server. Voice, video and screen sharing go through that community's media server and are not recorded by FFCom.
privacy.push: Notifications in the Android app. To tell you about messages while the app is closed, the app uses Google's Firebase Cloud Messaging. Your device registers its notification identifier with the central server. For each new channel message, the central server sends through Firebase the server and channel names, the author's name and up to 300 characters of the text; for direct messages, which are encrypted, only the sender's name is sent. This content is not stored on the central server and only passes through Google in transit (Firebase holds the message for up to 24 hours while the phone is offline). Every notification (channel, direct message and friend) also carries a temporary link to the sender's profile photo, which the app downloads from the central server. The link lasts up to 48 hours and uses a random identifier that can't be guessed.
privacy.pushControl: You can mute a server or a channel from its menu, turn off FFCom notifications in Android settings, or sign out, which removes the device from your account. In the browser and in the desktop app nothing goes through Firebase.

footer.egg: In online games, ff is the vote to forfeit the match. Also known as the day the crew hit FF and went off to build their own place.

e2e.setupBody: It protects the key that encrypts your direct messages. You'll type it once on each new device to read your history. Nobody can recover it for you, not even the people who run FFCom: if you forget it, your old messages become unreadable.

e2e.unlockBody: It unlocks the key for your direct messages on this device.
e2e.resetBody: Without the old phrase, your direct message history becomes unreadable on every device, and your other devices will ask for the new phrase. New messages work normally.

permission.title: Get notifications?
permission.body: FFCom lets you know about new channel messages, direct messages and friend requests even when the app is closed. Channel message text goes through Google's Firebase only to reach your phone; for direct messages, which are encrypted, only the sender's name and a temporary link to their photo are sent. You can mute a server or a channel from its menu.
